newsitem.title: FRANCE: Tietmeyer wants euro in 1999, unclear on delay.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer wants euro in 1999, unclear on delay.

text.p: German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Thursday the European Union should stick to the timetable for launching a single euro currency and he hoped France and Germany, as the two key states, would be ready.

But the head of the powerful and strongly independent German central bank remained ambiguous about the possibility of a delay to the planned launch on January 1, 1999, saying any such move would be for politicians, not central banks, to decide.

Tietmeyer's latest comments on European monetary union (EMU) came in a pre-recorded interview for French TF1 television for broadcast in a late-night show. A copy of the text, in French, was supplied in advance to Reuters.

Responding to questioning which attributed him with saying he could envisage a delay to the launch of the euro, Tietmeyer replied: "Unfortunately you have received erroneous information. I did not talk of a delay."
"I said that the treaty foresees a very clear calendar, a very clear date and a very clear rule for the taking of the decision," he said.

"But I said it would not be a catastrophe if there were a delay in this domain, but this only concerns the technical side. Concerning the timetable, it must be kept to. And if it has to be delayed, that's for the political authorities to decide, but certainly not central banks."

Tietmeyer said in Germany on Monday that a delay could be considered. "If it is the case that the big countries fail to meet the (Maastricht treaty) criteria, then a delay could be considered," he told a banking conference at that time.

In his Thursday comments, he said France and Germany were crucial to the launch of monetary union and, while the single currency should include more EU member states, this was not the case for other countries.

"I think that a monetary union would be possible only if Germany and France are part of it. This is not enshrined in the (Maastricht EMU) treaty, it's my opinion, and as far as I know, this opinion is shared to a large extent in Europe," he said.

"Therefore, it is a question of knowing whether the two economies are in a position where we can really launch the union. And I really hope this will be the case in spring of next year when it will be discussed and decided," he said.
"If one of the two countries were not part of it, monetary union could trigger conflict and this must not happen," he said.
Tietmeyer reaffirmed that he saw no reason for any change in German interest rates, but could not say now whether there was room for another cut.

Pressed on Germany's unemployment problems, he said the job of monetary policy was "to create good financial conditions for investments and to offer savers the possibility of getting appropriate interest."
"The problem is not a monetary policy problem," he said, adding that part of the jobless trouble was labour market rigidity and high employment costs.
German unemployment is near post-War record levels, although the latest data showed a decline in March in the unadjusted jobless rate to 11.7 percent from 12.2 percent the month before.

Tietmeyer said he was "generally satisfied" with prevailing exchange rates among major currencies and hoped the euro would be a stable and competitive currency versus what would be its main two rivals, the U.S. dollar and Japanese Yen.

"As regards the current exchange rate situation in Europe and overseas, we are generally satisfied. I hope, first of all, that the euro will be a stable currency that will be competitive with the two other currencies," he said.
